strengths: The decoupled atom-type and structure time axes provide a conceptually clean, useful unification of crystal structure prediction, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation in one model without task-specific retraining. This is a meaningful extension of multimodal flow modeling to periodic crystals.

The composition- and symmetry-aware ordering with hierarchical permutation augmentation is an intuitive crystallographic inductive bias for sequence-based Transformers. The gains are especially notable on the larger MPTS-52 benchmark, where MCFlow-L reaches 27.16% single-sample and 41.45% 20-sample CSP match rates.

The evaluation is unusually broad: two datasets, three generation settings, three model scales, 10,000-sample de novo evaluation, sampling-step studies, guidance sensitivity analysis, and thermodynamic, novelty, validity, and symmetry diagnostics.

De novo results are competitive across multiple criteria. MCFlow-B has the best reported average rank among CHGNet-evaluated models, while the models attain high compositional validity and favorable metastability rates. Reporting S.U.N./MS.U.N. usefully reveals that high stability alone does not imply discovery utility.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It provides algorithms, architecture sizes, optimization settings, inference settings, compute information, metric definitions, and an explicit—if brief—discussion of scaling limitations.
No material research-ethics issue is apparent. The impact discussion is proportionate to the domain and does not make harmful operational claims.
weaknesses: The discrete-flow formulation is mathematically inconsistent as written. Equations (22) and (24), Table 6, and Algorithm 1 define the CTMC rate vector as δ_{A0}(At)δ_{A1}/(1−t), whose entries sum to a positive value rather than zero. Consequently, δ_{At}+h u is not a normalized transition distribution. A negative diagonal/self-state term or an explicit off-diagonal-rate convention appears to be missing. Because CTMCStep is also unspecified, this affects the soundness and reproducibility of a central modality rather than being merely cosmetic.

The evidence does not isolate the claimed benefit of the proposed ordering. The key “−PosEmb” ablation removes positional embeddings, not the electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering while retaining comparable positional information. A random ordering, electronegativity-only ordering, Wyckoff-only ordering, and ordinary fixed ordering are needed. The cumulative permutation ablations similarly do not cleanly estimate each component's independent effect.

The paper does not compare the unified model against task-specific versions of the same architecture under matched parameter and training budgets. Comparisons to heterogeneous external baselines show competitiveness, but do not establish whether unification improves sharing, causes negative transfer, or offers a favorable compute/quality tradeoff.

The atom-type-generation evaluation is weak. MCFlow underperforms the deterministic CGCNN baseline in single-sample match rate on both datasets, and its advantage appears only with best-of-20 sampling, which is not compute-matched to the deterministic baseline. CGCNN's adaptation and training protocol are insufficiently described, and compositional validity alone does not establish chemically plausible site assignments.

Several empirical conclusions are stronger than their evidence. The assertion that ordering explains the MPTS-52 gains is not causally established; improved symmetry modeling is largely supported by plotted marginal histograms without quantitative distances or uncertainty; and no results include multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Thermodynamic claims rely on CHGNet relaxation and a described combination of Materials Project hulls with Matbench formation-energy references, but calibration and implementation details are limited. Baseline values are not uniformly available or clearly recomputed under one pipeline. Moreover, MCFlow's high raw metastability rates fall sharply after uniqueness and novelty filtering—for example, MCFlow-L reports 90.4% metastability but only 16.8% MS.U.N.—which tempers the discovery claim.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables: there is no stated code/model release, exact data split identifiers and random seeds are absent, symmetry/orbit preprocessing tolerances are not given, and the ODE solver and CTMC simulation rule are unspecified. Training times are reported only for the base model.

The limitations section acknowledges scaling to larger unit cells but omits important limitations exposed by the results: dependence on target-derived symmetry preprocessing during training, surrogate-energy false positives, low unique-and-novel yield, lack of uncertainty analysis, and the weak single-sample atom-type accuracy. Overall, the paper has clear promise, but the central discrete-process specification and evidential gaps require revision before others can reliably build on it.

strengths: Soundness: The decoupled atom-type and structure time axes provide a coherent way for one flow model to implement CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation. The manuscript gives probability paths, objectives, parameterizations, and inference algorithms. Review based on the complete manuscript and appendices: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d619143693d3434eb1d7369e2d10fa8c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Significance: A shared model for several crystal-generation directions is potentially useful, particularly if it can amortize training and share representations across tasks. Results on both MP-20 and the larger, chronological MPTS-52 benchmark are relevant.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates three model scales, reports CSP and de novo results against numerous prior systems, examines integration-step sensitivity, and includes component and guidance ablations.
Presentation: The main idea and task-specific trajectories are explained clearly, and the appendix supplies model sizes, loss weights, inference settings, metric definitions, and pseudocode.

The de novo results contain genuine positives: MCFlow has high structural and compositional validity, strong CHGNet-based metastability, and considerably better MPTS-52 CSP match rates than several non-template baselines.
weaknesses: Soundness: The principal claim about composition- and symmetry-aware ordering is not properly isolated. The purported ordering ablation removes positional embeddings, which changes the architecture and makes every ordering ineffective; it is not a comparison against random ordering, element-only ordering, Wyckoff-only ordering, or generic permutation augmentation. The cumulative inter/intra ablations likewise do not establish that crystallographic information, rather than regularization, causes the gains.

Soundness: Evidence that the model internalizes symmetry consists mainly of marginal histograms of space groups and Wyckoff statistics. No quantitative distribution distance, confidence interval, seed variation, per-composition analysis, or symmetry-validity/constraint-violation rate is reported. Similar marginals do not demonstrate correct conditional crystallographic structure.

Technical clarity: The discrete-flow equations are internally problematic or at least incomplete. Equations 22 and 24 describe a CTMC transition as delta_current plus a nonnegative rate vector whose entries do not sum to zero; the negative diagonal/self-transition term required for a valid generator is absent. CTMCStep is not defined sufficiently to determine whether the implementation silently repairs this issue.

Evaluation: Atom-type generation is weakly supported. Exact-match rates are only 1.20–3.32% for a single sample and are below the deterministic CGCNN reference. The claimed advantage comes from drawing 20 MCFlow samples while the deterministic baseline receives no comparable candidate budget. Compositional validity alone does not show that substitutions are chemically plausible, stable, or faithful to the conditioning structure.

Evaluation: The appendix's template-conditioned comparison is not controlled. Template-based baselines are conditioned on the target template, whereas MCFlow is post hoc filtered to generated samples matching that template; the survival/coverage rate is omitted. Conditional accuracy after filtering can therefore be inflated and is not comparable to actual template-conditioned generation.

Evaluation: De novo comparisons mix results and protocols from different systems. Only a subset is marked as using CHGNet relaxation, many entries are missing, and there is no uncertainty analysis. Direct uniqueness and novelty rates are omitted even though the sharp gap between metastability and MS.U.N.—for example, 90.4% versus 16.8% for MCFlow-L—suggests substantial duplication or training-set overlap. This undercuts the diversity narrative.

Significance and originality: Modality-specific time axes are adapted directly from established multimodal-flow work. The crystal-specific additions are potentially useful but incremental, and the paper does not compare the unified model against separately trained task models under matched total parameters, compute, or data. Consequently, it does not establish that unification improves accuracy, efficiency, or transfer rather than merely packaging several tasks into a 134M–464M parameter model.

Reproducibility: There is no code or checkpoint availability statement, and important details are missing: random seeds and repeated-run variation, exact split identifiers, symmetry-detection tolerance and preprocessing software, ODE solver and CTMC implementation, baseline execution provenance, and complete CHGNet relaxation/hull construction settings. Reporting up to 10,000 epochs without steps, stopping behavior, or total compute further limits replication.

Presentation: Several conclusions overstate the evidence—for example, attributing MPTS-52 gains to ordering without a direct ordering control and calling three model sizes with Pearson/Spearman correlations of exactly ±1 a scaling analysis. There are also minor editing defects such as duplicated text in Section 4.1.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations discussion mentions only larger unit cells. It does not address the lack of exact symmetry guarantees, dependence on surrogate CHGNet energies rather than DFT validation, database and elemental-coverage bias, low atom-type exact-match accuracy, mode collapse/duplication, or the safety implications of proposing unverified materials. The impact statement is promotional rather than a balanced risk analysis. No human-subject concern is apparent, but the treatment of scientific reliability and deployment limitations is inadequate.

strengths: Soundness: The decoupled time-axis formulation is a coherent way to support crystal-structure prediction, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation with one model. Periodic coordinates are handled on a torus, and the manuscript provides algorithms and modality-specific paths.

Evaluation: The paper covers two benchmarks, three tasks, three model scales, single- and multi-sample prediction, sampling efficiency, thermodynamic surrogate evaluation, and component/guidance ablations. MCFlow is competitive with task-specific methods and is especially strong on the larger MPTS-52 benchmark.

Significance: A reusable model spanning several crystal-generation directions is practically useful. The favorable symmetry distributions and reduced collapse toward P1 structures address a meaningful weakness of unconstrained all-atom generators.

Originality: Applying any-to-any multimodal flow to joint atom-type and periodic-structure modeling is a useful synthesis. The composition/symmetry-aware ordering and hierarchical orbit permutations are sensible crystal-specific additions.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is generally clear and well organized, with detailed architecture, optimization, inference, metric, resource, and algorithm descriptions. Limitations concerning larger unit cells are acknowledged.
weaknesses: Soundness: The discrete-flow notation appears mathematically incomplete. Equations 22–24 call u a CTMC rate vector, but the stated conditional vector is proportional only to the target point mass and therefore does not sum to zero; the negative diagonal/current-state term is not specified. Algorithm 2 likewise leaves CTMCStep undefined. The authors should clarify whether only off-diagonal jump intensities are represented and give the normalized transition rule.

The principal ordering claim is not cleanly isolated. Removing positional embeddings makes a Transformer unable to exploit any ordering, so that ablation does not distinguish the proposed electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering from arbitrary or simpler canonical orderings. Comparisons against random ordering, element-only ordering, Wyckoff-only ordering, and full permutation augmentation are needed.

Several causal interpretations are stronger than the evidence. Improved MPTS-52 results are attributed to ordering and augmentation without a controlled comparison, while the symmetry evidence is primarily a distribution plot without quantitative divergence, uncertainty, or tests across random seeds.

The atom-type-generation evaluation is weak: CGCNN is an unusual deterministic reference rather than a competitive conditional generator, its adaptation is insufficiently explained, and exact recovery of one held-out composition is questionable when the paper emphasizes that a structure may admit multiple valid compositions.

Baseline comparability is uneven. Many de novo baselines lack stability metrics, surrogate-relaxation protocols may differ, and the template-conditioned results filter MCFlow samples using the target template. Model sizes and training compute are also not controlled, despite the large model having 464M parameters.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive hyperparameters: no code or checkpoint availability is stated; dataset sizes and exact chronological split boundaries are missing; orbit-detection tolerances and preprocessing details are unspecified; and results have no seeds, confidence intervals, or variability estimates. Training for up to 10,000 epochs also warrants a clearer compute report.

The stability evidence relies on CHGNet rather than DFT and excludes failed relaxations from S.U.N.-style calculations, which may bias results. The limitations and impact discussions should also address surrogate error, computational cost, and risks of treating generated candidates as experimentally viable. Minor presentation defects include clipped running headers on several appendix pages.

strengths: Soundness: The two-time flow formulation is coherent and naturally realizes CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation as different inference trajectories. The paper provides conditional objectives, continuous/discrete parameterizations, inference algorithms, and an important ablation showing that coupling the time axes reduces MP-20 CSP match rate from 63.14% to 45.58%.

Significance: A single model handles three useful crystal-generation settings without task-specific retraining. Unified training nearly matches CSP-only training (63.14% versus 61.92% match rate), suggesting that this flexibility does not cause substantial negative transfer.

Evaluation: The study covers MP-20 and the larger, chronological MPTS-52 benchmark; includes single- and multi-sample CSP, standardized LeMat-GenBench evaluation, polymorph-aware metrics, scaling results, computational costs, and several component ablations. MCFlow is especially strong on MPTS-52 CSP and MLIP-estimated stability metrics.

Originality: Applying modality-wise flow times to joint discrete atom types and periodic continuous crystal structures is a useful synthesis. The electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering with restricted inter- and intra-orbit augmentation is a practically interesting transformer inductive bias.

Presentation and reproducibility detail: The manuscript is clear and well organized, with self-contained background, equations, pseudocode, metric definitions, architecture sizes, optimizer settings, priors, loss weights, integration steps, guidance parameters, and approximate hardware/runtime requirements. The limitations discussion honestly identifies the restriction to ordered crystals and the stability-novelty trade-off.
Ethics: No major research-ethics concern is apparent, and the claimed use is computational candidate generation rather than autonomous experimental deployment.
weaknesses: Soundness of the materials-quality claims is limited by reliance on MLIP-based stability rather than DFT validation. In the pre-relaxed comparison, MCFlow uses Orb-v3 for relaxation while Orb-v3 is also one member of the evaluation ensemble, creating a possible favorable alignment. Standard deviations across generated structures do not measure variability across training or sampling runs, and the reported SUN counts are small (13–26 for MCFlow), so several apparent differences may not be statistically robust.

The causal evidence for the proposed symmetry mechanism is incomplete. Table 5 uses cumulative ablations rather than a full factorial design, and the comparison between electronegativity ordering, atomic-number ordering, and unrestricted random permutation does not isolate Wyckoff ordering from hierarchical augmentation. Thus the claim that the gains specifically arise from internalizing crystallographic symmetry is stronger than the evidence warrants.

The method uses ground-truth space-group orbits and Wyckoff positions during preprocessing to construct its ordering and augmentation. Although it does not require a template at inference, this is still explicit symmetry-derived supervision; the manuscript should state more precisely how CSP and DNG sequences are initialized when the target Wyckoff partition is unavailable and temper language suggesting symmetry is learned without explicit symmetry information.

Atom-type generation is only weakly validated. Single-sample exact match rates are roughly 1–3%, the baselines are an adapted FlowMM and a deterministic CGCNN rather than strong task-specific generative methods, and compositional validity only checks heuristic charge-neutrality/electronegativity rules. The four substitution examples often reproduce the original material or entries already present in train/validation data and receive no energetic, DFT, or property validation, so the claim of physically meaningful substitution is preliminary.

De novo generation exhibits a substantial novelty trade-off: novelty falls from 52.2% for MCFlow-S to 18.6% for MCFlow-L after pre-relaxation, despite improving stability. This raises concerns about memorization or concentration near known structures and limits the discovery significance of the strongest stability results.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for independently rebuilding the results: no implementation or trained-model release is identified, random seeds and repeated-run variability are absent, and important preprocessing details such as symmetry-finding tolerances, exact split artifacts, CTMC stepping, and ODE solver choices are insufficiently specified. The stated clipping of training times to at most 0.9 also means conditional inference evaluates time embeddings at 1.0; this train–inference mismatch is not analyzed.

The limitations and impact discussion omits the lack of DFT or experimental validation, possible MLIP bias, empirical atom-count prior, and the risk that computationally plausible candidates may be mistaken for experimentally realizable materials. These omissions do not create a major ethical concern, but they should constrain the paper's discovery claims.

strengths: Soundness: The two-time formulation is coherent at a high level: independently evolving atom-type and structure variables give a principled way to realize CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation with one trained model. The CSP-only comparison in Table H.7 supports the claim that unified training does not materially harm CSP performance.

Evaluation breadth: The paper evaluates MP-20 and the larger, chronological MPTS-52 benchmark, uses LeMat-GenBench for de novo generation, reports multiple model scales, and includes computational-cost, guidance, ordering, permutation, and coupled-time ablations. MCFlow is particularly competitive on MPTS-52 CSP and on energy/stability metrics.

Methodological contribution: The composition- and symmetry-aware ordering with hierarchical permutation augmentation is a sensible, practically useful inductive bias for a non-equivariant Transformer. Tables 5 and H.4 provide evidence that the ordering and constrained augmentation improve performance over atomic-number ordering and unrestricted random permutations.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized. It supplies equations, pseudocode, architecture and training settings, metric definitions, computational resources, and a candid limitations section discussing applicability to ordered crystals and the stability-novelty trade-off.

Significance and originality: Applying modality-wise flow times to crystals is not conceptually new relative to prior multimodal-flow work, but combining this idea with crystal-specific ordering produces a useful unified system and introduces the relatively underexplored structure-conditioned atom-type direction.
weaknesses: Soundness: The discrete-flow exposition is formally inconsistent as written. Equations 22 and 24 call u a CTMC rate vector and write the transition probability as delta_x plus h*u, but the stated conditional u is nonnegative and does not sum to zero; the required negative diagonal or an explicit off-diagonal-rate convention is absent. CTMCStep is also left undefined. This may be repairable notation, but it prevents verification of a central component from the manuscript alone.

The atom-type-generation evidence is weak. Single-sample MCFlow has lower match rate than CGCNN on both datasets, while the favorable 20-sample results are not compared with top-k CGCNN or 20-sample FlowMM. Compositional validity is largely structure-independent, and the substitution study comprises only four hand-selected examples, often recovering the original element or entries appearing in training. It does not establish useful structure-conditioned substitution performance.

The symmetry claim is stronger than its evidence. Figure 4 compares aggregate marginal distributions without quantitative distances, uncertainty, or a measure of whether individual samples satisfy the intended high-symmetry constraints. Space-group determinability and avoidance of P1 collapse do not by themselves demonstrate that crystallographic symmetry has been learned correctly.

The de novo results reveal a serious stability-novelty trade-off: novelty falls from 52.2% for MCFlow-S to 25.4% and 18.6% for the base and large models, and stable-unique-novel rates remain only 0.5-0.7% after pre-relaxation. Thus the strongest stability numbers do not translate into a clearly superior discovery yield. Pre-relaxing MCFlow with Orb-v3, which is also part of the evaluation ensemble, further warrants a careful sensitivity or leave-one-potential-out analysis.

Experimental uncertainty is largely absent. The paper reports no repeated-training seeds or confidence intervals for CSP, ATG, or ablations; the standard deviations in Table 2 concern generated structures rather than training variability. Several claimed gains are small enough that run-to-run variation could change their interpretation. The cumulative ablation in Table 5 also does not independently identify each component's effect.

Comparisons do not fully disentangle the proposed ideas from scale and backbone capacity. MCFlow-B/L have 134M/465M parameters versus roughly 12M-28M for major CSP baselines, and there is no comparably sized DiT control with conventional ordering or a task-specific DiT baseline across all tasks. The results therefore do not establish how much of the gain comes from multimodal flow, ordering, or raw capacity.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful configuration tables: no code or model-release statement is provided, and random seeds, exact dataset split identifiers, preprocessing/symmetry tolerances, library versions, optimizer details, ODE/CTMC update rules, and baseline checkpoint/evaluation provenance are missing. The stated 10,000-epoch maximum also sits uneasily with plots ending at 5,000 epochs and an underspecified checkpoint-selection procedure.

Significance and originality are moderate rather than decisive. Independent modality time axes are adapted from existing multimodal flow frameworks, while the main crystal-specific novelty is an ordering/augmentation heuristic that depends on ground-truth crystallographic analysis during preprocessing and does not apply to disordered or amorphous systems. The phrase “any-to-any modality generation” overstates evaluation involving only two modality groups and three trajectories.

Ethics and limitations: No immediate human-subject, privacy, or dual-use concern is apparent, and the stated limitations should not be penalized. However, the impact discussion would benefit from acknowledging the environmental cost of 134M-465M models trained for thousands of epochs and the risk of treating MLIP-predicted stability as experimentally validated materials discovery.

strengths: Soundness: The decoupled atom-type and structure time axes are technically well motivated, and the conditional flow objectives, manifold treatment of fractional coordinates, CTMC formulation for atom types, and task-specific inference trajectories are described coherently. The coupled-time ablation is particularly persuasive: MP-20 CSP match rate falls from 63.14% to 45.58%.

Soundness: The evaluation is unusually broad, covering CSP, de novo generation, atom-type generation, polymorph-aware matching, symmetry distributions, scaling, computational cost, and component ablations on MP-20 and the larger chronological MPTS-52 benchmark. MCFlow is especially convincing on MPTS-52 and on stability-related LeMat-GenBench metrics.

Originality: Applying multimodal flow with independent time axes to unified crystal modeling is a useful synthesis, while the electronegativity/Wyckoff ordering and hierarchical inter-/intra-orbit augmentation provide a novel, practical symmetry bias without requiring structural templates at inference.

Significance: A single model supporting CSP, de novo generation, structure-conditioned atom typing, and masked substitution without retraining is valuable. Unified training matches CSP-only training, suggesting that this flexibility does not incur an evident performance penalty.

Presentation: The paper is well organized and generally clear. Figures effectively explain the two-dimensional inference trajectories and symmetry-aware ordering, while the appendices supply algorithms, metrics, hyperparameters, resource requirements, and additional comparisons.

Reproducibility and ethics: The manuscript specifies architectures, losses, priors, optimizer settings, checkpoint selection, inference steps, guidance parameters, metric tolerances, and hardware. It also gives an honest limitations discussion covering disordered systems and the stability-novelty trade-off. The stated applications raise no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical claims lack uncertainty across independent training and sampling runs. Reported standard deviations in de novo generation describe variation across generated structures rather than seed-to-seed uncertainty, so small differences—such as the CSP gains over OMatG or the 70.7% versus 70.5% polymorph-aware METRe result—cannot be judged statistically significant.

The atom-type-generation evidence is less compelling than the CSP and de novo results. In single-sample match rate, MCFlow remains below deterministic CGCNN on both datasets; its advantage appears mainly under a 20-sample budget. The substitution study uses only four selected materials and lacks a systematic held-out evaluation, so the broad claim of learning physically meaningful substitution patterns is only suggestively supported.

The symmetry-distribution evidence is mostly visual. Quantitative distribution distances, uncertainty, and sensitivity to the 0.1 Å SpaceGroupAnalyzer tolerance would better support the claim that MCFlow captures crystallographic symmetry rather than merely avoiding P1 collapse.

The paper provides detailed implementation specifications but does not state that code, trained checkpoints, exact data splits, preprocessing artifacts, or random seeds will be released. Reproducing the full study would also require multiple recent MLIPs and substantial computation, including up to 464M parameters and 2–4 days for the base model.

The stability-novelty trade-off is substantial: with pre-relaxation, novelty decreases from 52.2% for MCFlow-S to 18.6% for MCFlow-L, and SUN remains below 1%. Thus, the strong stability numbers should not be interpreted as equally strong discovery of stable, unique, novel materials. Using Orb-v3 for MCFlow pre-relaxation while Orb-v3 also participates in the evaluation ensemble additionally deserves a clearer fairness or sensitivity analysis.

The conceptual novelty is meaningful but not foundational: independent modality-wise time axes adapt established multimodal-flow ideas, and several method components derive from existing continuous/discrete flow machinery. The contribution is best viewed as a strong domain-specific integration rather than a new generative principle.

The limitations section is candid but incomplete: it does not discuss dependence on symmetry extraction and numerical tolerances, MLIP bias in stability assessment, the limited substitution validation, or the environmental cost of large-model training.
